notes.written: Written 19 Oct 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: An energy shock is lifting inflation

Brent oil is around $106 and WTI near $98 after attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and strikes in the Gulf. Headline inflation is up almost everywhere: US 3.7%, euro area 3.8%, Australia 4.0%, New Zealand 4.1%, UK 3.1% (3.4% expected).
Central banks have turned to raising rates
In six weeks the RBNZ (2 Sep), ECB (10 Sep), Fed (16 Sep), BoJ (18 Sep) and RBA (29 Sep) all raised rates. The Bank of England held but is split, while the Bank of Canada and SNB are holding.
Hiring is weakening: US payrolls +29,000 in September, Canada −68,300, Australia −39,300. Consumers are gloomy (US sentiment 46.3), even where they are still spending.
RBNZ, Bank of Canada and the Fed on 28 Oct, the ECB on 29 Oct and the BoJ on 30 Oct, plus Australia’s CPI, US GDP and core PCE inflation, the UK Autumn Forecast Statement and Canada’s budget.
Higher real rates are hurting gold and silver
With US 10-year yields near 5.1% (about 2.8% after inflation), gold is down about 15% in six months and silver about 30%, despite record central bank gold buying.

USD.note: Raised on 16 Sep, the first rise since 2023. Officials pencil in one more rise this year.

EUR.note: Raised in June and on 10 Sep. Says inflation will stay well above target for an extended period.

GBP.note: Held on 17 Sep for the sixth meeting in a row, but 3 of 9 members voted to raise to 4%.

JPY.note: Raised on 18 Sep to the highest since 1995. Two members dissented and the Governor gave no clear signal of more, so the yen fell.

CAD.note: On hold for six meetings while others hike: underlying inflation is near target and jobs are being lost.

AUD.note: Raised on 29 Sep, unanimously, and said it could go further if needed.

NZD.note: Raised twice (to 2.75% on 2 Sep), but signalled a more measured pace, which knocked NZD lower.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged; growth support comes mostly from the government.

stories.USD: Inflation has turned back up: consumer prices rose 3.7% on a year in September and producer prices jumped 1.3% in a single month. So the Fed raised rates on 16 September for the first time since 2023. Underneath, hiring has slowed sharply (only 29,000 jobs added in September, unemployment 4.2%) and households are gloomy (sentiment 46.3), yet they keep spending (retail sales +0.8%). Borrowing costs are high: the 10-year yield is about 5.1%, and about 2.8% after inflation. Next: Fed decision 28 Oct, GDP and the Fed’s preferred inflation measure 29 Oct.
stories.EUR: Energy has pushed euro-area inflation to 3.8% (2.5% without food and energy), and the ECB has raised rates twice to a 2.50% deposit rate. Growth is holding up (GDP +0.6% in Q2, services surveys at 53), but investors are gloomier (ZEW 25.8, down from 31.4), consumers are downbeat (−17) and the trade balance has swung to a deficit (−€6.8bn) as the energy import bill grows. Next: flash business surveys 23 Oct, ECB 29 Oct.
stories.GBP: Inflation is rising again: 3.1% in August, with 3.4% expected for September, mostly from fuel. The Bank of England is close to raising rates: it held at 3.75% on 17 September, but three of nine members voted for 4%. UK data have recently beaten forecasts more than anyone else’s (GDP +0.1% in August against −0.1% expected, retail sales +0.5%), though unemployment is 4.9% and pay growth is cooling (3.9%). Government borrowing costs are high (10-year gilt about 5.2%). The Autumn Forecast Statement on 28 Oct sets out the government’s tax and spending plans, a big moment for the pound.
stories.JPY: The Bank of Japan raised rates to 1.25% on 18 September, the highest since 1995, but the yen still fell because the decision was split and gave no clear hint of more. With US rates near 4%, the interest-rate gap still favours the dollar (USD/JPY around 158). Price pressure is building: Tokyo’s core inflation jumped to 2.7% in September. Households are cutting back (spending −3.1% on a year), while big manufacturers are confident (Tankan +24). Next: BoJ 30 Oct.
stories.CAD: The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% for six meetings while others raise rates. Underlying inflation is near target (median 2.0%, trimmed 1.9%), even though headline inflation is 3.0% because of petrol. Jobs are going fast: 68,300 lost in September after 41,700 in August, and unemployment is 6.5%. High oil prices help Canada’s exports (trade surplus C$4.2bn). Next: CPI 19 Oct, federal budget 27 Oct, BoC 28 Oct.
stories.AUD: The RBA raised rates to 4.60% on 29 September and said it could go further, with inflation at 4.0% and households expecting 5.3%. But the economy is softening: 39,300 jobs lost in September, unemployment up to 4.7%, household spending flat and business confidence negative (NAB −13). Australian data have mostly missed forecasts this month. China, Australia’s biggest customer, is slowing (4.3% growth) with weak shoppers. Next: September CPI 28 Oct.
stories.NZD: The RBNZ has raised rates twice, to 2.75%, after inflation hit 4.1% in Q2 on petrol and diesel. In September it said further rises would come at a more measured pace, and NZD fell. The economy is weak: GDP +0.2% in Q2, unemployment 5.6%, retail volumes down and a wide trade deficit (NZ$1.97bn in September). Next: Q3 CPI 21 Oct (UK evening), RBNZ 28 Oct.
stories.CHF: Switzerland is the outlier: inflation is only 0.8% (August), and the SNB holds at 0% and stands ready to sell francs if needed. The franc is a safe haven that tends to gain when global worries rise. The economy is strong: GDP jumped 1.5% in Q2 (1.9% including big sporting events), factories are still expanding (PMI 55.3), shoppers are spending (retail +3.2% on a year) and unemployment is low at 3.1%.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Growth slowed to 4.3% in Q2, shoppers are weak (retail sales +0.4% on a year) and inflation is low (0.9%), while exports are strong (trade surplus $133.5bn in September). Factory surveys sit just above 50.

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Up about 17% in six months. The Middle East conflict is the main driver: tanker attacks near Oman and the Strait of Hormuz and strikes on Saudi targets in early October raised fears for supply. Any easing, or more output from OPEC+, would pull prices back.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Down about 15% in six months. Rising real interest rates (the US 10-year yield after inflation is near a multi-year high) and a firmer dollar are the headwinds. Central banks buying record amounts (288.9 tonnes in Q2) and safe-haven demand during the conflict are the support.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Down about 30% in six months, roughly double gold’s fall: the same rate headwind, plus worries about factory demand as growth slows.
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
